To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a long dispersed repeat sequence that comprises approximately 6% of the human genome is transcribed into a heterogeneous population of high molecular weight RNA molecules, some of which contain a poly(A) tract, and the complementary RNA molecules are discretely and heterogeneously sized.
a substantial fraction of human cytoplasmic and nuclear RNAs are complementary to a long, dispersed, repeat sequence that is present in both human and mouse DNAs.

approximately 1% of the heterogeneous nuclear RNA from cultured human lymphoblastoids is complementary to a dispersed repetitious sequence of human DNA, and that some of this RNA is discretely sized, some is heterogeneously sized, and some is poly(A)-terminated.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification, isolation and characterization of discrete and heterogeneous high molecular RNA species that are complementary to dispersed repeats of human DNA.
the characterization of the RNA complementary to a long repetitious sequence that is dispersed throughout the human genome.
the identification of a family of dispersed repeat elements of human DNA and with the characterization of the RNA transcripts complementary to this family.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the dispersed repetitive sequence of human DNA is a candidate for a transposon, and its RNA is a candidate for an mRNA, although the latter conclusion is not yet definitive.
the dispersed repetitive sequences of human DNA, as defined by the complementary RNAs, are transposable genetic elements that are present in a high copy number in human DNA.
the dispersed repeat sequence is a possible transposon, and that the complementary RNAs are the transposon transcripts, some of which may be translated.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have found a long dispersed repeat in human DNA, which is transcribed into heterogeneous and discretely sized RNAs in human lymphoblasts, and which is also transcribed into heterogeneous RNA in mouse cells.

a long dispersed repeat sequence in human DNA is transcribed in the nucleus to produce both heterogeneously sized and discretely sized RNAs and that some of the discrete RNA molecules are transported into the cytoplasm, where they are not associated with ribosomes.
the long dispersed repeat family in human DNA appears to be a transposon.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the human dispersed repetitive sequence, which we call the human Alu repeat, is transcribed into heterogeneous and discretely sized RNAs that are present in both the nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments of the cell.
the dispersed repeat sequence appears to have a complex and possibly transposon-like structure and is transcribed in a complex manner in human and mouse cells.
the human genome is much more active than previously believed, and this is a very important finding for the field of cancer research.
